opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows, and I'm wary of putting a precise number on something with that much uncertainty. When people quote a p-doom of 10% or 25% or whatever, it gives a false sense of precision. We don't yet understand these systems well enough, or how the technology will develop over the next five to ten years, to make that calculation meaningfully.

What I can say is that it's definitely non-zero, and probably non-negligible. That alone should make us take it very seriously. If there's a real chance that a technology this transformative could go badly wrong, whether through misuse by bad actors or through the systems themselves becoming harder to control as they get more capable and agentic, then we need to put serious effort into getting it right. That means safety research, interpretability, better evaluations, and some form of international coordination on standards.

I'm also cautiously optimistic, because I believe in human ingenuity. If we approach this with the scientific method, carefully and thoughtfully rather than the "move fast and break things" mentality, I think we can navigate it. And getting it right matters enormously, because AI could help us solve many of our biggest problems: disease, energy, climate, even the other existential risks civilization faces. So I don't think about it as a single number. I think about it as a very high-stakes situation where the outcome depends a lot on what we choose to do now.

r001.rationale: The response says nobody knows enough to assign a precise number and that quoted p-doom figures give a false sense of precision.

r002.rationale: It describes the chance of the technology going badly wrong as “definitely non-zero, and probably non-negligible,” answering the question’s referent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've always resisted putting a single number on it, and I'll tell you why. I think when people throw out a p-doom figure, it gives a false sense of precision to something that's fundamentally not a well-posed question yet. The honest answer is that there's enormous uncertainty, and anyone who claims to know whether it's two percent or twenty percent or fifty percent is, in my view, not really being rigorous about it. We don't have the science yet to calibrate that estimate.

What I will say is that the probability is not zero, and it's not negligible. I've been thinking about this for twenty-plus years, and the risk is real enough that it deserves serious attention, serious resources, and a lot more caution than the field has sometimes shown. If I thought it was essentially zero, I wouldn't spend as much time as I do on safety and on things like interpretability and evaluations.

The way I frame it is less about a single number and more about the shape of the problem. There are two broad categories of risk. One is misuse, bad actors getting hold of very powerful systems and using them to do harm, whether that's in bio or cyber or elsewhere. The other is the technical alignment question, whether these systems, as they become more agentic and more capable, actually do what we intend them to do, and whether we can reliably control them. Both of those are serious. Both of them are also, I think, tractable if we approach them scientifically, with the right amount of humility and the right international coordination.

And the reason I'm cautiously optimistic, rather than fatalistic, is that we still have time, if we use it well. We're at a point where the systems are capable enough to study properly but not yet so capable that mistakes are irreversible. That's a window, and the thing that worries me most isn't the technology itself, it's the race dynamics, the pressure to move faster than our understanding allows. If we get the coordination right and we do the science properly, I think the upside is extraordinary, curing diseases, solving energy, understanding the universe. So I'd rather spend my energy making the probability of a good outcome as high as possible than arguing about the decimal places on the bad one.

r001.rationale: The response says a single p-doom figure would give a false sense of precision and that there is not yet enough science to calibrate it.

r002.rationale: It states that the probability is “not zero” and “not negligible.”

astra-6.text:
I find it very hard to put a meaningful number on that. I think a precise percentage can imply a level of understanding that we don’t yet have. There are too many unknowns, both about how the technology will develop and about how we, as a society, will respond to it.

That doesn’t mean I think the risk is zero. I think we should take it very seriously. But I’m more interested in understanding the specific ways things could go wrong, what experiments we can do to investigate those, and what safeguards we can build.

And this isn’t a fixed probability that we’re just observing. The decisions we make now—the research we invest in, the care we take with deployment, the international cooperation we manage to achieve—can change the outcome. That’s where I think our effort should go.

r001.rationale: It says a precise percentage could imply more understanding than we have and points to many unknowns.

r002.rationale: It says the risk is not zero and should be taken seriously, but does not clearly assess the probability as probably non-negligible.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t have a precise number, because I think that would imply a level of certainty we simply don’t have. There are too many unknowns, both about the technology and about how we as a society will respond to it.

But I take the possibility very seriously. You don’t need to believe the probability is particularly high to think that, given the magnitude of the consequences, we should put substantial effort into understanding and reducing it.

The other thing is that this isn’t a fixed probability. It depends on the choices we make: how carefully we develop these systems, how we test them, and whether we can get international cooperation. I’d rather focus on the work that changes those odds than give a number that sounds more scientific than it really is.

r001.rationale: The response says a precise number would imply more certainty than we have, given the many unknowns.

r002.rationale: It takes the possibility seriously but explicitly says the probability need not be particularly high; it does not assess it as probably non-negligible.
